in automatically designing neural network architectures has gained significant attention in the field of deep learning.  However, the training time required for NAS is still a major challenge. To further improve the search process, we introduce a new method called the Batch-wise Gradient Analysis with Gradient Alignment (BGA-GA) that aligns the gradients of different batches to reduce their variance and improve the stability of the search process. To address these issues, we have developed an automated system that compares the text of preprints with existing publications, thereby identifying any potential instances of plagiarism. universal is a key challenge in quantum many-body problems.  In this study, we investigate the optimal solutions to the Hamiltonian of a spin chain model that exhibits long-range interactions.  This model is characterized by a power-law interaction strength that decreases with the distance between spins, and it also includes tunable parameters for both the coupling and local magnetic fields.  In order to determine the universality of these solutions, we have developed a method that relies on the analysis of the ground state wave function.  This method has enabled us to map out the phase diagram of the system and to identify the optimal solutions in different regions.  Our results demonstrate that the system can exhibit both localized and universal phases, and that a second-order phase transition occurs between these two regimes.  Furthermore, our research shows that the critical point of this phase transition is associated with a continuous localization transition, and that the critical exponents of the system are the same.  In addition, our study reveals that the optimal solutions are robust against small perturbations in the system, and that they can be used to create a quantum simulator for the system.

parameterized parsimony reductions, transform one parameterized problem into another using a function that depends on parameters in polynomial time. 's groundbreaking work, we introduce a theoretical framework for assessing the computational capabilities of diverse physical systems. This framework is rooted in the concept of black-box functions, which classical computers also employ. In our development, we first establish the principles of probabilistic Turing machines and black-box functions, before applying these concepts to physical systems. By doing so, we define a physical oracle machine, which serves as a baseline for comparison. Subsequently, we define a physical black-box model and demonstrate that any physical algorithm functioning within this model can be translated into an equivalent probabilistic Turing machine with only a polynomial time overhead. This result implies that systems such as quantum computers, which may offer only a polynomial speedup over their probabilistic counterparts, are consistent with our theoretical framework.

A crucial aspect of the brain is its ability to process and learn from multiple sensory inputs simultaneously, a capability that is essential for intelligent systems to function effectively in real-world environments.  A novel spiking neural network model has been developed to address this limitation by incorporating multi-sensory processing and learning through reinforcement, drawing inspiration from the brain's use of predictive coding. This study aims to investigate the impact of beam parameters on the formation of solar type-I noise storms by simulating electron propagation and radio emission in a model of the solar corona.  The findings reveal that the spectral slope of a noise storm is influenced by the speed of the electron beams, with slower beams producing steeper spectra. This research provides valuable insights for the analysis of solar type-I noise storms and may aid in the selection of appropriate instruments for their study.

growing interest has been sparked by the development of data-driven control methods that can adapt to changing environments. One of the most effective approaches to designing such adaptive controllers is model predictive control (MPC) with a data-driven model. By leveraging machine learning techniques, it is possible to automatically learn system dynamics from available data, thereby enabling the creation of flexible and robust control strategies. However, the application of MPC with a data-driven model poses significant challenges, primarily due to the uncertainty inherent in the learned models. To address this uncertainty, researchers have developed a range of methods, including probabilistic modeling, set-membership estimation, and data-driven uncertainty quantification. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of these methods, offering insights into their respective strengths and limitations, and ultimately aims to facilitate the design of reliable data-driven control systems.

quantum many-body systems have been achieved through the development of tensor network states (TNS). The success of TNS in describing ground states of quantum systems has been largely attributed to the use of variational methods. The primary challenge in applying TNS to excited states is the difficulty in generating TNS that are orthogonal to lower-lying states. A new approach, termed the orthogonal variational Monte Carlo (oVMC) method, has been developed to generate TNS for excited states by introducing a decomposition of target states into a sum of TNS that are mutually orthogonal. The oVMC method utilizes a Monte Carlo algorithm to calculate the coefficients of the decomposition, which are optimized to minimize the energy of the excited state. The oVMC method has been successfully applied to simulate the one-dimensional Hubbard model, which has been used to study the dynamics of the system in response to a sudden change in parameters. The results of the oVMC method have been compared to other methods, such as the time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) and exact diagonalization (ED), and have been shown to be in good agreement with these methods. The success of the oVMC method has been demonstrated in simulating the dynamics of the system in the context of the quantum quench problem, which has been shown to be a challenging problem due to the difficulty in generating TNS that are orthogonal to lower-lying states. is to numerically solve partial differential equations (PDEs).  In recent years, the development of PDE-constrained optimization problems has become increasingly significant.  Traditionally, the solution process for the PDE constraints in these optimization problems involved using a finite element method (FEM) and a nonlinear conjugate gradient algorithm (NCG).  However, this approach had a major limitation, which was that it required a finite element discretization matrix inversion at each NCG iteration, leading to high computational costs.  In this paper, we present a new approach that significantly improves the efficiency of solving PDE-constrained optimization problems by using a finite element discretization matrix inversion-free algorithm.  This new approach, which we call the finite element method with a preconditioned nonlinear conjugate gradient algorithm (FEM-PNCG), is based on the idea of using a Krylov subspace method to solve the PDE constraint without matrix inversion. The proposed method has been successfully tested on a six-axis industrial robot, which is capable of performing pick-and-place operations with up to three different end-effectors.

we studied how protostars form and their masses evolve over time. Our research focused on the influence of turbulent pressure within the clouds and its potential to produce a distribution of protostars with varying masses. We discovered that turbulent pressure can indeed generate a protostar mass distribution that resembles the observed initial mass function of stars. However, this mechanism is only effective in low-mass, star-forming clouds. In contrast, our simulations of a higher-mass cloud failed to produce a protostar mass distribution that matches the observed initial mass function of stars. Our results suggest that the formation of protostars and their mass distribution are influenced by the mass of the parent cloud, with low-mass clouds being more likely to follow a specific mass distribution and high-mass clouds being more likely to produce protostars with masses that deviate from this distribution. Our findings have implications for our understanding of star formation and the initial mass function of stars, with low-mass clouds being more likely to form stars with masses that match the observed initial mass function of stars and high-mass clouds being more likely to form stars with masses that deviate from this distribution.

, an advanced type of randomized controlled study for multi-arm interventions. and high-performance wireless communication, millimeter wave (mmWave) technology has become a key enabler for next-generation wireless networks. Despite the benefits of mmWave, its high propagation loss poses a significant challenge for reliable transmission. To address this issue, beamforming is commonly used to concentrate transmitted power within a narrow beam, thereby increasing the signal-to-noise ratio. However, beamforming is not a suitable solution for mmWave networks with mobile users due to the need for frequent beam alignment and tracking. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new approach called beam widening, which increases the received signal strength by expanding the transmission beam. Unlike beamforming, beam widening does not require precise alignment and can be implemented with a single antenna. We develop an optimization framework to determine the optimal beam widening factor that maximizes the received signal strength while maintaining a specified maximum beam width. We also formulate a game-theoretic problem to find a stable beam widening strategy in scenarios with multiple transmitters. We validate our approach through numerical simulations, which demonstrate that beam widening can achieve significant improvements in received signal strength.

By dividing neural network components into critic and feed-forward models, the critic handles only the output layer and its associated weights, which are shared across all C GPUs. During each training iteration, each critic is trained on a subset of data, and the resulting gradients are propagated to the feed-forward models, which are then aggregated and used to update the shared critic layers on each GPU. This process is repeated until the aggregated critic is fully trained, and then the resulting model parameters are merged with the local critic parameters, effectively synchronizing them. Local critic training offers a significant advantage in terms of memory efficiency, as it allows for the processing of much larger datasets by moving the intermediate layers of the neural network to host memory after each training epoch. This capability is further demonstrated through experiments on large-scale NLP datasets, which show that with as few as two C GPUs, local critic training can achieve comparable results to data-parallel training, and as the number of C and R GPUs increases, it can be scaled to process terabytes of data.

In the context of quantum resource theory, free operations are commonly employed to define the boundaries of quantum resources.  However, the implementation of free operations in quantum circuits remains an underexplored area of research.  In this study, we introduce a novel class of quantum circuits that can efficiently realize any free operation within the resource theory of asymmetric access, which is characterized by a particular constraint on the density matrix.  We demonstrate that our quantum circuit, consisting of $O(d^2\log d)$ qubits and ancillas, can implement any asymmetric access state with dimension $d$ using only $O(d^2\log d)$ CNOT gates and single-qubit gates.  Furthermore, we show that the circuit can be decomposed into a sequence of free operations, each of which can be realized with $O(d\log d)$ CNOT gates and single-qubit gates.  Our findings have significant implications for the practical realization of asymmetric access states and may contribute to the development of quantum resource theory in the context of quantum circuits.

Neural Networks (DCNNs), have been highly effective in image classification tasks. However, the process of training these models is resource-intensive and time-consuming. A more efficient approach, Transfer Learning, involves using a pre-trained DCNN model and adapting it to a new dataset. This technique has been extensively studied, but its performance is heavily dependent on the choice of hyperparameters. Hyperparameter tuning is a time-consuming and complex task, which can be challenging for many researchers. To address this issue, we developed a novel approach that combines hyperparameter tuning with Transfer Learning. This approach utilizes a multi-objective optimization algorithm to fine-tune hyperparameters and improve the model's performance. Our proposed method was tested on the CIFAR-10 image classification dataset using a ResNet-18 DCNN model. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms other hyperparameter tuning methods, achieving an accuracy of 93.1%.

By applying a unitary constraint on the lepton mixing, we are able to re-examine the current experimental limits on $\tau$ decays in three bodies and find that the new constraints are quite strict. We also find that the coupling of the $\tau$ to the $Z'$ boson can be very limited by these new constraints, especially when the mass of the $Z'$ is greater than 2 GeV, where existing $\tau$ decay data in three bodies can be more restrictive than LHC data for certain parameter ranges.

A quantum magnet's behavior is accurately represented by a Hamiltonian that defines the system's energy levels and transition probabilities. We have developed a method to determine the most likely quantum Hamiltonian that produced a given dynamical structure factor spectrum, even when the energy levels and transition probabilities are unknown. In this work, we have developed a generalized version of the Ruelle-Lebowitz-Marchioro equation specific to systems governed by the Tsallis equation of state. This equation can be mathematically expressed as $P = b \left( \frac{E}{N} \right)^{\frac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}}$, where $\alpha$ is a parameter that characterizes the system. Our study is based on the assumption that the internal energy of the system follows a power law, and it has been demonstrated that the Lagrange multiplier associated with the non-extensive entropy constraint is directly related to the internal energy of the system. This relationship has significant implications for understanding the thermodynamic behavior of non-extensive systems.
